newsitem.title: USA: Russia's Mars probe likely to hit Australia - U.S..
newsitem.headline: Russia's Mars probe likely to hit Australia - U.S..

text.p: By Gene Gibbons)

A disabled Russian space probe is expected to fall to Earth in east-central Australia at about 8:12 p.m. EST on Sunday (0112 GMT Monday), but damage is likely to be minimal, a senior White House official said.

U.S. National Security Council official Robert Bell said the expected impact zone for the Mars probe, which has four small batteries powered by radioactive plutonium, was "in the central to eastern part of Australia, which would be somewhere north of Canberra."
The six-tonne spacecraft lifted off from Kazakhstan's Baikonur space centre on Saturday, but failed to break out of the Earth's orbit after a booster rocket misfired.

Bell told reporters with President Bill Clinton on a trip to Asia that if the probe fell to Earth just one minute later than expected, the debris would plunge into the Pacific Ocean "somewhere east of Australia.

The craft was expected to burn up on re-entering Earth's atmosphere, Bell said in a telephone conference call from Washington. But two landing vehicles were expected to survive and crash in a relatively uninhabited region of Australia.

NASA officials said the vehicles were built to survive a landing on Mars and weighed 110 pounds (50 kilos) each. Two 6.5-foot (2-metre) penetrators designed to ram into the surface of Mars and weighing 143 pounds (65 kilos) each, were also expected to survive re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere.
The landing vehicles each carried two tiny plutonium batteries about the size of 35mm film canisters containing a total of 200 grams of the radioactive material.

"The Russian space agency has informed NASA that these batteries are designed to withstand great heat and great stress on impact," Bell said. He said Russian assessments that there was little danger of radioactive contamination of the environment was "very reassuring."
Clinton, who conferred by telephone with Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Sunday morning about the situation, is scheduled to begin a five-day visit to Australia on Monday.
Bell said Clinton had offered Howard "assets we have in the Department of Energy" to deal with any mishaps.
The Russian probe had been due to reach Mars on Sept. 12 next year. The failed mission was the second of three planned trips from Earth to Mars in just over a month.

The United States launched a robot voyage to Mars two weeks ago and a second mission will blast off on Dec. 2. All were tasked to check for signs of water on the far-away planet -- a key clue to whether there was once life on Mars.
Bell said a misfiring of a fourth stage of the probe's booster rocket had doomed the Russian Mars probe.
Bell said there were "a couple of scenarios that could be a worst case," but stressed all were "extremely unlikely."
One was that the plutonium canisters would break up. If this happened at high altitude, Bell said a small radioactive cloud that would result would dissipate harmlessly.

"If some cloud of dispersal were formed at a lower altitude and inhaled by humans, it could be lethal," Bell said. He said there could also be a localised danger if the canisters broke up upon impact.

"But again, we're talking about a very modest amount of plutonium ... a total of about 200 grams. And it's hard for me to imagine that even if it's diffused into some sort of small cloud that it would be a very large area covered by this," said Bell, who is a special assistant to the president and a senior director of the NSC for defence policy.

The Russian space mishap was the fourth incident of its kind in recent years. A U.S. space vehicle called Skylab and plunged to earth over Western Australia in 1979 without causing damage and a Russian Cosmos satellite fell in an unhabited region of Canada in 1987.
In 1991 the Soviet space station Salyut 7 re-entered the Earth's atmosphere and the debris was believed to have landed in the Atlantic Oceon, though some pieces were reportedly found in Argentina.
